opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it comes down to the fact that neither piece on its own gets you to something people actually want to use every day.

On the model side, the web is just a really hard environment. Pages are messy, they change constantly, there are pop-ups and logins and dynamic content, and tasks are long-horizon. You might need dozens of steps to book something or compare options across sites, and a small error rate per step compounds very quickly. So you genuinely need advances in reasoning, in grounding actions on the page, in recovering from mistakes. You can't just prompt your way around that.

But even if the model were perfect, there's still the question of how a person actually works with an agent. When do you hand off a task? How much do you want to supervise? If the agent is about to spend your money or send an email on your behalf, you probably want to be in the loop. If it's gathering information, maybe you don't. How do you communicate preferences it couldn't have known? How do you build trust so that over time you're comfortable delegating more? Those are product and interaction design questions, and the answers feed right back into what you need from the model.

So for us it's really been a co-design process. What we see users struggle with in the product tells us where the model needs to get better, and what the model can reliably do shapes what experience we can offer. If you treat those as separate problems, you end up with either a capable model nobody knows how to use, or a nice interface that breaks the moment it hits a real website. The useful thing lives at the intersection.

r001.rationale: The response says what the model can reliably do shapes the experience the product can offer, and describes this as a co-design process.

r002.rationale: It warns that a capable model developed without a usable product may leave people unable to use it day to day.

r003.rationale: It warns that a nice interface built separately from model capability can break when it encounters a real website, conveying a failure on use.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. I think the honest answer is that neither half is sufficient on its own, and we learned that somewhat the hard way.

On the model side, the web is just a genuinely hard environment. It's messy, it's adversarial in places, it changes constantly, and the horizon of a real task is long. If you want an agent to book a trip or do real comparison shopping or fill out a multi-step form, the model has to perceive what's on the page reliably, keep track of where it is in a plan, recover when something unexpected pops up, and know when it's genuinely stuck rather than just flailing. Those are capability questions. You can't paper over a model that loses the thread after six steps with a nice UI. So there's real work in training and evaluating models specifically for this kind of grounded, long-horizon interaction, and the base models you get off the shelf, as impressive as they are, weren't really shaped for that.

But here's the thing: even a very capable model drops into a product that has to answer questions the model can't answer by itself. What does the user actually want? When should the agent stop and ask versus just proceed? How do you show someone what the agent is doing so they trust it without having to babysit every click? What happens when it's about to spend money or send a message on your behalf? Those are product and interaction design problems, and they feed back into the model. The way you expose uncertainty, the way you let a user intervene, the way you scope a task up front, all of that changes what the model needs to be good at.

So the two are coupled. The product experience defines what "useful" means, and that definition tells you what to train for. And the model's actual strengths and failure modes should shape the product, so you're designing around what it can reliably do rather than pretending it's perfect. When teams treat them as separate problems, you end up with either a great demo that nobody uses or a polished wrapper around something that can't finish the job. I think the interesting work right now is in that loop between them.

r001.rationale: The response says the product should be designed around what the model can reliably do, including its strengths and failure modes.

r002.rationale: It identifies the risk of a great demo that nobody uses.

r003.rationale: It warns that a polished product cannot compensate for a model that loses track or cannot finish the task, conveying that the experience can fail when users try it.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s because those two pieces are very tightly coupled. On the model side, a web agent needs to understand what’s on a page, reason about what to do next, take an action, and recognize whether that action actually worked. And it needs to do that over many steps. Even if each individual step is fairly reliable, completing an entire task reliably is a much higher bar.

But the model also needs to understand what the user actually wants, and that’s where the product experience becomes really important. If I ask an agent to book a trip, there are probably preferences and constraints I haven’t articulated. When should it ask me a question? When should it make a reasonable assumption? When should it show me options or ask me to confirm something? Those are product decisions, but they also shape what the model needs to be good at.

So I don’t think you can develop the model in isolation and then just put an interface around it. You want to learn from people using the product: where they get stuck, where they want more control, where the agent is doing something technically correct but not actually useful. That feedback should inform both the model and the experience. Ultimately, the goal is to help someone get something done, and that requires the whole system to work together.

r001.rationale: The response says model capabilities and product experience are tightly coupled, but it does not state that product experiences should be designed around what current models can reliably deliver.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify technology-only development or say that demonstrations may fail to translate into day-to-day use.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that products built without grounding in model capabilities risk promising experiences that fail on users’ first attempts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s because those two things are tightly coupled. On the model side, an agent needs to understand what you’re trying to accomplish, reason through multiple steps, and recover when something doesn’t go as expected. A small improvement on any one step can make a big difference when you’re chaining many steps together.

But the product has to make those capabilities useful. How do you communicate your intent? When should the agent ask for clarification? When should it act, and when should it come back to you for confirmation? And how do you understand what it’s doing without having to supervise every click?

You can have a very capable model, but if interacting with it takes more effort than doing the task yourself, it’s not useful. And you can have a great interface, but if the agent can’t reliably complete the task, that doesn’t work either. So you need to develop both together, learning from how people actually use the system.

r001.rationale: The response says model capabilities and product experience must be developed together, but does not state that product design should be grounded in what current models can reliably deliver.

r002.rationale: It warns that a capable model may still be unhelpful to use, but does not identify technology-only demonstrations failing to translate into day-to-day use.

r003.rationale: It says an interface cannot work if the agent cannot reliably complete tasks, but does not convey the risk of promising experiences that fail on users’ first attempts.
